reading.rtitle: What the Committee Is Actually Scoring
paras: Every executive program says it reads the whole file, and most of them mean it. What they do not say is that the reading is done against a rubric: a sheet with six criteria on it and a threshold under each one. Most candidates picture a committee arguing about them for an hour. In the applicant pool of a large program, hardly any file gets an argument. Two readers score it separately, and a handful of files go to a third reader because the two scores are far apart. The word readers use for a file that clears every threshold and excites nobody is box-checking: every box checked, and not one reason to remember the name.

The six criteria are not equal, and the sheet says so. Progression and scope of responsibility carry the most weight; the test score carries the least, and a few programs have stopped asking for it at all. Readers are told to weigh each criterion against the others rather than add them up, which is why a low score in one place can be offset by an unusual strength somewhere else. Almost all applicants in a given year look similar across the board -- good grades, good employers, good English -- and that similarity is the problem, not the standard. The well-rounded file is the one that rarely gets remembered, because virtually every file in the pool is well-rounded.

Two things end a file early, and neither of them is a weakness. The first is a claim nobody can check. The second is an answer that contradicts the rest of the file: none of the six criteria is about perfection, but all of them are about consistency. Beyond those two deal-breakers, few things are fatal. There is one caveat, and readers repeat it every year: the criterion most candidates ignore is the one about what they would bring to the class, and hardly anybody answers it with anything except ambition. Most applicants clear the bar on paper. The ones who are admitted clear it on one criterion so clearly that the reader can say, in a sentence, what the class would lose without them.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 text, written for this lesson from the criteria sheets published by executive MBA admissions offices

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: Most of the files in that pool come from consulting and banking. Mine does not.
Hardly any applicant in my year has run a construction company with a hundred and fifty people on site.
A handful of our projects are delivered late, and I can tell you which ones and why.
Few of my decisions are made alone, but the ones that cost money are.
Virtually all of my management was learned on site, and none of it in a classroom.
None of the six criteria is about my title, and that is good news for me.

listenings.text: People imagine a room, and there is a room, but it comes later. What happens first is a sheet with six criteria on it and a number under each one, and two of us read your file against it separately. Most of the differences between the two of us are half a point. Now, the part candidates get wrong: the six lines are not equal, and they are not added up. Progression and scope of responsibility carry more weight than anything else, and the test score carries the least. A few programs here have stopped asking for it. What I am doing is weighing one line against another, so a low number in one place is not a problem if something in the file offsets it. And the files that worry me are the ones with no low number anywhere. Almost all of them look the same: good grades, good employer, good English, and nothing I can remember by Friday.

I was rejected the first year and admitted the second, with a better job in between, and I do not think the job is what changed it. The first time, five of my six answers were fine. The sixth one, the one about what I would bring to the class, I answered with ambition. I wrote about what I wanted to learn. Hardly any of that is useful to a committee, because every file in the pool wants to learn. The second time I wrote about the thing none of them had. I had rebuilt a factory line in a country where I did not speak the language, and I named the two months when it nearly failed. Most of my file did not change at all. One paragraph changed, and it was the paragraph that told them what the class would lose if I were not in it.
